learn: Every person is special. You have a name, a birthday and things you like to do.
Some people like to paint. Some like to run. Some like to read. What do you like?
Being yourself is a good thing.
check: Does every person have something special about them?
Which is something you might like to do?
lessons.try: Draw a picture of something you love to do.

learn: People are alike in some ways. We all need food, sleep and friends.
People are different in some ways. We may look different, speak different languages or like different foods.
Differences make the world interesting. We treat everyone with kindness.
check: We all need food and sleep
We all have the same name
We all like the same food
How do we treat people who are different from us?
lessons.try: Find one way you and a friend are alike and one way you are different.

learn: It is good to know your full name.
It is good to know a trusted grown-up's phone number, so you can get help if you are lost.
Keep this information private online. Only share it with trusted grown-ups, police or teachers.
check: Why should you know a grown-up's phone number?
So you can get help if you are lost
To call anyone on the internet
Who can you share your phone number with?
What should you know about yourself?
lessons.try: Practise saying your full name and a grown-up's phone number with a family member.

learn: Everyone has a name. Your name tells people who you are.
You also have an age. Most kindergarteners are five or six years old.
Say your full name and age clearly, so people can understand.
check: When you say your name, speak...
lessons.try: Practice saying: My name is ___ and I am ___ years old.

learn: Our bodies help us do many things: run, jump, hug and think.
We take care of our bodies by eating healthy food, sleeping and washing.
Every body is different, and every body is good.
check: We take care of our bodies by...
lessons.try: Trace your body on big paper. Label your head, arms, hands, legs and feet.

learn: We all have feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared and excited.
All feelings are okay. What matters is what we do with them.
When you feel angry, you can take deep breaths and use words.
lessons.try: Make faces for five feelings in a mirror.

learn: Everyone likes different things: foods, colors, games and animals.
Sharing what you like helps others know you.
It is fun to find friends who like the same things.
check: Does everyone like the same things?
Sharing what you like helps others...
Finding friends who like the same things is...
lessons.try: Draw your favorite food, color and animal.

learn: You can do many things now that you could not do as a baby.
You can walk, talk, draw, count and maybe tie your shoes.
Every day you learn something new.
check: Could you walk as a newborn baby?
lessons.try: Make a list with a grown-up of five things you can do now.

learn: You are growing. Your feet, hands and body get bigger.
You also learn new things and change what you like.
Growing up takes time.
check: As you grow, your body gets...
What else changes as you grow?
lessons.try: Compare your hand to a baby picture or to a grown-up's hand.

learn: Your address tells where you live: a number, a street and a town.
Knowing your address and a grown-up's phone number helps you if you get lost.
Only share them with safe grown-ups like police officers or teachers.
check: Who is safe to tell your address if lost?
Knowing a phone number helps if you get...
lessons.try: Practice saying your address and a grown-up's phone number.

learn: Your birthday is the day you were born.
Every year on your birthday you turn one year older.
There are 12 months. Your birthday is in one of them.
check: Your birthday is the day you were...
On your birthday you get one year...
How many months are in a year?
lessons.try: Find your birthday on a calendar. Which month is it?

learn: Friends are people we like to play with and who are kind to us.
Good friends share, take turns and say sorry.
You can make a new friend by saying hi and asking them to play.
check: To make a friend you can...
Say hi and ask to play
lessons.try: Draw you and a friend doing something fun together.

learn: At school we learn, play and help each other.
We have a teacher, classmates and a classroom.
Each person in the class is special.
check: Who helps us learn at school?
Each person in the class is...
lessons.try: Draw your classroom and the people in it.

learn: An all-about-me book shows who you are.
Each page can tell something: my family, my favorite food, what I can do.
You are the author, so write your name on the cover.
check: Who is the author of your all-about-me book?
lessons.try: Make a four-page all-about-me book.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: All About Me
learn: You know your name, age, birthday and address.
You know your feelings are okay and how to handle them.
You are special, and so is everyone else.
check: When you feel scared, you can...
Your birthday is the day you were...
lessons.try: Share your all-about-me book with the class or your family.

learn: A family is a group of people who love and care for each other.
Families come in many sizes. Some have one parent, some have two, some live with grandparents, aunts or foster parents.
Every kind of family is a real family.
check: People who love and care for each other
Do all families look the same?
Can a grandparent be part of a family you live with?
lessons.try: Draw the people in your family.

learn: Family members help each other.
They share chores like setting the table, feeding a pet or putting toys away.
When everyone helps, the work is done faster and there is more time to play.
check: So the work is done faster
lessons.try: Choose one chore to do for your family today.

learn: A tradition is something a family does again and again, often on special days.
A tradition could be a special meal, a song, a game or a story told every year.
Traditions help families remember and feel close.
check: Something a family does again and again
lessons.try: Ask a grown-up about a tradition in your family.

learn: Families come in many kinds. Some are big and some are small.
Some children live with a mom and dad, some with one parent, grandparents, two moms, two dads or other relatives.
What makes a family is that they love and care for each other.
check: Can grandparents be part of a family?
lessons.try: Draw the people in your family.

learn: Family members have names for each other: mother, father, sister, brother, grandma, grandpa, aunt, uncle, cousin.
Your parent's sister is your aunt. Your aunt's child is your cousin.
Some families are joined by adoption, and that is a real family.
check: Is a family joined by adoption a real family?
lessons.try: Name the members of your family and how they are related to you.

learn: Family members help each other with chores, cooking and cleaning.
Everyone can help, even small children.
Working together makes the work easier.
lessons.try: Help with one chore at home today.

learn: Families play games, read books, go to parks and share meals.
Spending time together helps families feel close.
Every family has its own favorite things to do.
check: Spending time together helps families feel...
Which is something families do for fun?
Does every family have the same favorites?
lessons.try: Tell your favorite thing to do with your family.

learn: Families have rules to keep everyone safe and happy.
Rules might be: brush teeth, be home by dinner, use kind words.
Following family rules shows respect.
lessons.try: Tell two rules your family has.

learn: Family history is the story of your family over time.
Grandparents can tell stories about when they were young.
Old photos show how your family looked long ago.
check: Family history is your family's story over...
Who can tell stories about long ago?
Old photos show how your family looked...
lessons.try: Ask a grandparent or older relative about their childhood.

learn: A family tree is a drawing that shows family members.
Grandparents are at the top, then parents, then children.
It looks like a tree with branches.
check: Who is often at the top of a family tree?
A family tree looks like a tree with...
lessons.try: Make a simple family tree with your parents and grandparents.

learn: Families everywhere love each other, but they live in different ways.
Some families live in apartments, some in houses, some on farms, some on boats.
They eat different foods and speak different languages.
check: Do families eat the same foods everywhere?
lessons.try: Look at pictures of families from other countries. What is the same as yours?

learn: Families change. A new baby may be born, or someone may move away.
Changes can feel exciting or hard.
Talking about feelings helps families through changes.
lessons.try: Draw a change your family has had.

learn: We show love with hugs, kind words, helping and spending time together.
Saying thank you and I love you makes family members feel good.
Love is something we do, not just say.
check: Saying thank you makes people feel...
lessons.try: Do one kind thing for a family member today.

learn: Many families have pets like dogs, cats, fish or birds.
Pets need food, water, exercise and love.
Taking care of a pet teaches responsibility.
lessons.try: Draw a pet you have or would like, and list what it needs.

learn: Families come in many kinds and change over time.
Families work together, have rules, have fun and love each other.
Family history and family trees tell our family's story.
lessons.try: Tell three things you learned about families.

learn: Rules tell us how to act.
Rules keep us safe and help things be fair.
Without rules, games and classrooms would be confusing.
check: Keep us safe and make things fair
lessons.try: Name a rule from a game you play.

learn: At school we raise our hand to talk, so everyone gets a turn.
We walk in the hall, so nobody gets hurt.
We keep our hands to ourselves and use kind words.
check: Why do we raise our hand to talk?
How do we move in the hall?
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up why we walk in the hall.

learn: There are rules at home too, like washing hands before eating or putting toys away.
If someone breaks a rule, there can be a consequence. A consequence is what happens because of a choice.
A good consequence can come from a good choice, too, like a clean room and more space to play.
check: What happens because of a choice
Can a good choice have a good consequence?
lessons.try: Talk with a grown-up about one rule at home and why it matters.

learn: When the teacher talks, we look and listen.
Listening helps us learn and stay safe.
Show listening with eyes watching, ears listening and mouth quiet.
lessons.try: Play Simon Says to practice listening.

learn: In class we raise a hand to speak.
This way everyone gets a turn and no one talks over others.
Wait until the teacher calls your name.
check: Raising hands lets everyone get a...
lessons.try: Practice raising your hand and waiting at dinner.

learn: We walk inside the school, not run.
Running can cause falls and bumps.
Outside on the playground is the place to run.
lessons.try: Practice walking feet down a hallway at home.

learn: Sharing means letting others use things too.
Taking turns means waiting while someone else goes first.
Sharing and turns make play fair.
check: If a friend wants your toy, you can...
lessons.try: Play a board game and take turns.

learn: We keep our hands and feet to ourselves.
Hitting, pushing and kicking hurt others.
If someone hurts you, tell a grown-up.
check: Before hugging, it is kind to...
lessons.try: Practice asking: May I have a hug? before hugging.

learn: When we finish, we clean up our space.
Toys go back on shelves. Trash goes in the can.
A clean room is safe and easy to use.
lessons.try: Clean up your room and put each toy in its place.

learn: We line up to go places together.
Stand behind the person in front, face forward, and keep a little space.
Lining up keeps everyone together and safe.
check: In line we keep a little...
lessons.try: Line up your toys in a straight line.

learn: A fire drill is practice for leaving the building safely.
When the alarm rings, stop, line up quietly and walk out.
Go to the meeting place outside and stay with your teacher.
check: When the fire alarm rings, we...
lessons.try: Practice a fire drill at home with your family.

learn: Many rules are for safety: wear a seatbelt, look both ways, wear a helmet.
Safety rules protect our bodies.
Grown-ups make safety rules because they care about us.
lessons.try: Name three safety rules you follow.

learn: A fair rule is the same for everyone.
If the rule is one turn each, then everyone gets one turn.
Fair rules help everyone get along.
check: One turn each means everyone gets...
lessons.try: Make one fair rule for a game with friends.

learn: Classes often make rules together.
Everyone shares ideas and votes on the best ones.
When we help make rules, we want to follow them.
check: To choose rules, a class can...
When we help make rules, we want to...
lessons.try: Help your family make one new rule for your home.

learn: Rules keep us safe and make things fair.
At school, we listen, raise hands, walk, share and clean up.
Breaking rules has consequences.
lessons.try: Draw a picture of one school rule and one home rule.

learn: A citizen is a member of a community, like a town or a country.
Good citizens help others and follow rules.
Even children can be good citizens at home and at school.
lessons.try: Name one thing a good citizen does.

learn: Good citizens are kind. They share, take turns and help.
Good citizens tell the truth, even when it is hard.
Kind words and honest words build trust.
check: What do kind and honest words build?
lessons.try: Do one kind thing for someone today.

learn: Parks, libraries and classrooms are shared places.
Good citizens take care of them. They throw trash away and keep things clean.
When we disagree, we use calm words and listen to each other.
check: How do we take care of shared places?
lessons.try: Pick up three pieces of litter with a grown-up's help.

learn: Responsible means doing your jobs without being reminded.
You can be responsible by feeding a pet, packing your bag or cleaning up.
People trust responsible people.
lessons.try: Choose one job to do every day this week.

learn: Respect means treating others the way you want to be treated.
We listen, use kind words and respect others' things.
We respect people who are different from us.
check: Respect means treating others how you want to be...
Should we respect people who are different?
lessons.try: Say please and thank you all day long.

learn: Being fair means everyone has a chance.
Fair players follow rules and do not cheat.
If you lose, say good game.
check: Being fair means everyone has a...
lessons.try: Play a game and say good game at the end, win or lose.

learn: Being brave means doing the right thing even when it is hard.
You can be brave by trying something new or standing up for a friend.
Brave people can still feel scared.
check: Being brave means doing the right thing when it is...
Standing up for a friend is...
lessons.try: Tell about a time you were brave.

learn: Good citizens help others.
You can help a friend who falls, help carry things, or share.
Helping makes our community better.
check: If a friend falls, you can...
lessons.try: Find one way to help someone at school or home.

learn: Honesty means telling the truth.
When we make a mistake, we tell the truth and say sorry.
Honest people are trusted.
check: When we make a mistake, we...
The boy who cried wolf learned to...
lessons.try: Read or listen to The Boy Who Cried Wolf. What did he learn?

learn: Including means inviting others to join.
Notice someone playing alone and ask them to play.
Everyone wants to belong.
check: If someone plays alone, you can...
lessons.try: Invite someone new to play with you.

learn: When we disagree, we use words, not hands.
Say: I feel ___ when you ___. Please ___.
Listen to the other person and find a fair solution.
lessons.try: Practice: I feel sad when you take my toy. Please ask first.

learn: Voting is a fair way for a group to decide.
Everyone gets one vote. The choice with the most votes wins.
Grown-ups vote for leaders like the president.
check: Voting is a fair way to...
lessons.try: Have your family vote on a dinner or a game.

learn: Leaders help groups make decisions and solve problems.
Your teacher is a leader in class. The principal leads the school.
The mayor leads a town, and the president leads the country.
lessons.try: Be a leader: help a group clean up or plan a game.

learn: Volunteers help without being paid.
They clean parks, help at food banks and visit older people.
Volunteering makes the community stronger.
lessons.try: Help a neighbor or donate toys you no longer use.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Good Citizens
learn: Good citizens are responsible, respectful, fair, honest and kind.
They help others, include everyone and solve problems with words.
You can be a good citizen every day.
check: A fair way for a group to decide is...
lessons.try: Make a good citizen badge and wear it while doing a kind act.

learn: A community is a place where people live, work and play together.
A community has homes, shops, schools, parks and roads.
People in a community help each other.
check: A place where people live, work and play together
lessons.try: Draw a map of three places in your community.

learn: Firefighters put out fires and help in emergencies.
Police officers help keep people safe and help if you are lost.
Crossing guards help children cross the street.
check: Who can help if you are lost?
Who helps children cross the street?
lessons.try: Act out how a firefighter helps.

lessons.t: Helpers Who Give Us What We Need
learn: Doctors and nurses help us stay healthy. Teachers help us learn.
Farmers grow food. Grocery workers sell it. Mail carriers bring letters and packages.
Every job helps the community in some way.
lessons.try: Ask a grown-up what job they do and how it helps others.

learn: Firefighters put out fires and rescue people.
They wear special gear to stay safe from heat and smoke.
They also teach us about fire safety.
check: If your clothes catch fire, you...
lessons.try: Practice stop, drop and roll.

learn: Police officers help keep communities safe.
They help people who are lost or in trouble, and make sure people follow laws.
If you are lost, a police officer can help.
check: If you are lost, you can ask a...
Police officers make sure people follow...
lessons.try: Draw a police officer helping someone.

learn: Doctors and nurses help us stay healthy and get better when we are sick.
They give checkups, shots and medicine.
A checkup checks your height, weight, eyes and heart.
lessons.try: Play doctor with a toy and give a checkup.

learn: Teachers help us learn to read, write, count and more.
Librarians help us find books and information.
Both love to help children learn.
check: Both teachers and librarians help children...
lessons.try: Thank a teacher or librarian with a card.

learn: Mail carriers bring letters and packages to our homes.
They walk or drive a route every day, in rain or snow.
Letters need an address and a stamp.
check: A letter needs an address and a...
lessons.try: Write a letter to a family member and mail it.

learn: Farmers grow food and raise animals.
They plant crops, care for cows and chickens, and harvest food.
Much of the food we eat comes from farms.
check: Much of our food comes from...
lessons.try: Find three foods in your kitchen that came from a farm.

learn: Grocers sell food in stores. Shopkeepers sell clothes, toys and tools.
We pay money for the things we buy.
Stores help us get what we need.
check: We pay ___ for things we buy.
Stores help us get what we...
lessons.try: Play store with toys and pretend money.

learn: Builders make houses, schools, roads and bridges.
They use tools like hammers, drills and big machines like cranes.
They wear hard hats to protect their heads.
check: A tall machine that lifts heavy things is a...
lessons.try: Build a house with blocks and name the tools a real builder uses.

learn: Sanitation workers collect trash and recycling.
They keep our streets clean and healthy.
Without them, trash would pile up everywhere.
lessons.try: Wave to the trash truck or thank a sanitation worker.

learn: Bus drivers take people to school and work.
Pilots fly airplanes. Train engineers drive trains.
They help people travel safely.
lessons.try: Draw a vehicle and the helper who drives it.

learn: Each helper uses special tools.
A doctor uses a stethoscope. A firefighter uses a hose. A mail carrier uses a mailbag.
Tools help people do their jobs well.
lessons.try: Match tools to helpers: hose, stethoscope, mailbag, hammer.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Community Helpers
learn: Community helpers keep us safe, healthy, fed and learning.
Each helper has a job and special tools.
When you grow up, you can be a community helper too.
check: Who helps us when we are sick?
lessons.try: Tell what helper you want to be and why.

learn: Needs are things we must have to live.
We need food, water, clothing and shelter.
A shelter is a safe place to live, like a house or an apartment.
check: Do we need food to live?
lessons.try: Name the four needs.

learn: Wants are things we would like to have, but we can live without them.
Toys, treats and games are wants.
It is fine to have wants. We just take care of needs first.
lessons.try: Sort pictures into needs and wants.

learn: People work to earn money. They use money to buy needs first, then some wants.
We cannot have everything we want. We have to make choices.
Saving means keeping some money for later, to buy something bigger.
check: Can we have everything we want?
lessons.try: Pretend you have 5 coins. What need and what want would you choose?

learn: A need is something we must have to live. Food is a need.
Our bodies need healthy food to grow and have energy.
Fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins are healthy foods.
lessons.try: Draw a healthy plate with fruit, vegetables, grain and protein.

learn: We need clean water to drink every day.
We need clothing to keep us warm, dry and safe.
Clothes change with the weather.
check: Do clothes change with the weather?
lessons.try: Choose clothes for a hot day and a cold day.

learn: Shelter is a safe place to live, like a house or apartment.
Shelter protects us from rain, cold and heat.
Homes come in many kinds around the world.
lessons.try: Draw your home and one home from another place.

learn: A want is something nice to have but not needed to live.
Toys, candy, games and new shoes we do not need are wants.
Wants are fine, but needs come first.
lessons.try: Sort pictures into needs and wants.

learn: Sometimes we must think hard. A coat is a need in winter. A third coat is a want.
Water is a need. Soda is a want.
Ask: Can I live without it?
check: To decide, ask: can I live...
lessons.try: Look around your home. Find three needs and three wants.

learn: Goods are things people make or grow that we can buy.
Bread, shoes, books and bikes are goods.
Goods can be touched.
lessons.try: Find five goods in your kitchen.

learn: Services are jobs people do for us.
A haircut, a doctor's checkup and a bus ride are services.
We pay people for their services.
lessons.try: Name three services your family uses.

learn: Money is used to buy goods and services.
Coins and paper bills are money. Pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters are coins.
People earn money by working.
lessons.try: Look at coins. Name a penny, a nickel, a dime and a quarter.

learn: Saving means keeping money for later instead of spending it now.
A piggy bank helps you save.
Saving helps you buy something bigger later.
lessons.try: Make a piggy bank from a jar and save coins.

learn: We cannot have everything we want. We must choose.
If you have one dollar, you might choose a book or a toy, but not both.
Thinking about needs first helps us choose well.
check: Can we have everything we want?
If you can buy one thing, you must...
lessons.try: Pretend you have 5 coins. Choose what to buy from a pretend store.

learn: Some people do not have enough for their needs.
We can share food, clothes and toys with others.
Giving to others helps the community.
lessons.try: With a grown-up, give food or clothes you do not need.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Needs and Wants
learn: Needs are food, water, clothing and shelter.
Wants are nice extras.
We use money to buy goods and services, and we save and share.
lessons.try: Make a poster with needs on one side and wants on the other.

learn: A map is a drawing of a place seen from above, like a bird would see it.
A map can show a room, a town, a country or the whole world.
Maps help us find our way.
check: A drawing of a place from above
A room, a town or the whole world
They help us find our way
lessons.try: Draw a map of your bedroom from above.

learn: Maps use small pictures called symbols. A tree symbol can mean a park.
The key tells what each symbol means.
Colours mean things too: blue for water, green for parks.
check: Small pictures that stand for things
lessons.try: Add symbols and a key to your bedroom map.

learn: A globe is a round model of Earth.
Blue shows water. Other colours show land.
Earth has big pieces of land called continents. We live in North America. Earth also has huge oceans.
check: What does blue show on a globe?
lessons.try: Find your continent and an ocean on a globe or map.

learn: A map is a drawing of a place from above, like a bird would see it.
Maps help us find where things are and how to get there.
There are maps of rooms, towns, countries and the whole world.
check: A map shows a place from...
Is there a map of the whole world?
lessons.try: Look at a map of your town with a grown-up.

learn: You can make a map of your own room.
Draw it from above: your bed is a rectangle, your rug is a circle.
Put each thing where it really is.
check: A map of a room is drawn from...
A bed on a map might be a...
On a map, put things where they...
lessons.try: Draw a map of your bedroom.

learn: A map key tells what the symbols mean.
A tree picture might mean a park. A blue line might mean a river.
Always look at the key to read a map.
check: A map key tells what ___ mean.
A blue line on a map often means a...
To read a map, look at the...
lessons.try: Make a map key for your bedroom map.

learn: The four main directions are north, south, east and west.
On most maps, north is at the top.
A compass rose on a map shows the directions.
check: On most maps, north is at the...
How many main directions are there?
Which shows directions on a map?
lessons.try: Find the compass rose on a map. Point north.

learn: Left and right help us give directions.
Hold up your left hand: your thumb and pointer make an L.
Turn left at the corner means go the way of your left hand.
check: Your left hand makes the letter...
Turn left means go toward your...
Left and right help us give...
lessons.try: Give someone directions to the kitchen using left and right.

learn: A school map shows classrooms, the office, the library and the playground.
Maps help new students find their way.
Fire drill maps show the way out.
check: A fire drill map shows the way...
lessons.try: Draw a map of the way from your classroom to the lunchroom.

learn: Earth has land and water.
On maps and globes, land is often green or brown, and water is blue.
There is more water than land on Earth.
check: Is there more water or land on Earth?
Land on a globe is often...
lessons.try: Look at a globe. Is there more blue or green?

learn: The big areas of water are oceans. The big areas of land are continents.
There are seven continents. We live on North America.
The Pacific Ocean is the biggest ocean.
lessons.try: Find North America and the Pacific Ocean on a globe.

learn: Mountains are very tall land. Rivers are long flowing water. Lakes are water with land all around.
Maps use symbols for each one.
The Grand Canyon in Arizona was carved by the Colorado River.
check: A lake has ___ all around it.
A long flowing water is a...
The Grand Canyon was carved by a...
lessons.try: Make a mountain, river and lake out of play dough or sand.

learn: You live in a town or city, in a state, in a country.
Our country is the United States of America.
There are 50 states, and Arizona is one of them.
lessons.try: Say your town, state and country.

learn: Treasure maps show a path to the treasure.
Follow the steps: start here, walk to the tree, turn right, dig at the X.
Following maps is like following directions.
check: On a treasure map, X often marks the...
A path on a map shows...
lessons.try: Hide a toy and draw a treasure map for a grown-up.

learn: Maps show places from above with symbols and a key.
Globes show the whole Earth: land, water, continents and oceans.
Directions help us find our way.
check: A map key tells what ___ mean.
A globe is shaped like a...
lessons.try: Make a treasure map with a key and a compass rose.

learn: The past is what already happened. Yesterday is in the past.
The present is now. Today is the present.
The future is what has not happened yet. Tomorrow is in the future.
lessons.try: Say one thing you did yesterday, one thing you are doing today and one thing you will do tomorrow.

learn: Long ago, life was different. People used candles and oil lamps before electric lights.
Many people travelled by horse or wagon. Clothes were washed by hand.
Children played with simple toys like hoops, marbles and dolls.
check: What did people use before electric lights?
How did many people travel long ago?
Which toy did children play with long ago?
lessons.try: Ask a grandparent or older person what toys they played with.

learn: Some things are still the same today. People still live in families, cook food and play games.
Some things changed. We have cars, computers and electric lights.
Learning about the past helps us understand today.
check: What is still the same today?
lessons.try: Draw a kitchen long ago and a kitchen today.

learn: Long ago, many homes had no electricity.
People used candles and fireplaces for light and heat.
Some families lived in log cabins or sod houses.
check: Long ago, people used ___ for light.
A log cabin is made of...
Did many homes long ago have electricity?
lessons.try: Compare a picture of a log cabin with your home.

learn: Long ago, many children went to one-room schoolhouses.
Children of all ages learned together with one teacher.
They wrote on small chalkboards called slates.
check: A one-room schoolhouse had how many rooms?
In one-room schools, children of all ages learned...
lessons.try: Write your name on a small chalkboard or paper slate.

learn: Long ago, people walked, rode horses or traveled in wagons.
Trips that take hours now took days or weeks.
Today we have cars, trains and airplanes.
check: Which is a way we travel today?
lessons.try: Draw a wagon and a car. How are they different?

learn: Long ago, many clothes were sewn by hand at home.
Girls often wore long dresses, and boys wore overalls or short pants.
Today most clothes are made in factories.
check: Long ago, many clothes were made...
Today most clothes are made in...
lessons.try: Look at old photos and describe the clothes.

learn: Long ago, families grew much of their own food.
They kept food cold in iceboxes or cellars, not refrigerators.
Today we buy most food at stores.
check: Long ago, food was kept cold in...
Today we buy most food at...
lessons.try: Ask a grandparent what they ate as a child.

learn: Long ago, toys were often made of wood, cloth or tin.
Children played with tops, marbles, dolls and hoops.
Today we also have electronic toys.
check: Long ago toys were often made of...
Which is a toy from long ago?
lessons.try: Play a game children played long ago, like marbles or jacks.

learn: Long ago, people wrote letters to talk to faraway friends.
Later came the telegraph and the telephone.
Today we use cell phones and video calls.
check: Long ago, people talked far away by...
lessons.try: Write a letter to a faraway relative.

learn: Long ago, many people were farmers, blacksmiths or shopkeepers.
A blacksmith made horseshoes and tools from iron.
Today there are new jobs, like computer programmers.
lessons.try: Draw a job from long ago and a job from today.

learn: A timeline shows events in order.
The earliest event is at the left. The newest is at the right.
You can make a timeline of your own life: born, walked, talked, started school.
check: The earliest event is at the...
Which comes first in your life?
lessons.try: Make a timeline of four things in your life.

learn: Grandparents and older people remember long ago.
Their stories teach us history.
Ask questions: What did you play? What was school like?
lessons.try: Interview an older person with three questions.

learn: Some things change a lot over time, like phones and cars.
Some things stay the same, like families, friends and play.
Change happens slowly over many years.
lessons.try: Name one thing that changed and one that stayed the same.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Long Ago and Today
learn: Life long ago was different: homes, schools, travel, toys and jobs.
Some things are the same: families, friends and learning.
Timelines and grandparents' stories teach us history.
lessons.try: Make a long ago and today poster.

learn: We live in a country called the United States of America.
A symbol is a picture or thing that stands for an idea.
The American flag has 50 stars and 13 stripes. The stars stand for the 50 states. The stripes stand for the first 13 colonies.
check: How many stars are on the American flag?
What do the 13 stripes stand for?
A picture or thing that stands for an idea
lessons.try: Count the stripes on a picture of the American flag.

lessons.t: The Bald Eagle and the Statue of Liberty
learn: The bald eagle is the national bird. It stands for strength and freedom.
The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor. It welcomes people to the country.
She holds a torch high to light the way.
check: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
What does the Statue of Liberty hold up?
lessons.try: Draw the Statue of Liberty holding her torch.

lessons.t: The Pledge and the Liberty Bell
learn: Many classrooms say the Pledge of Allegiance to show respect for the country.
The Liberty Bell is an old bell in Philadelphia. It has a big crack.
Symbols help people remember important ideas, like freedom and being together.
check: What is special about the Liberty Bell?
lessons.try: Find the Liberty Bell in a picture. Can you see the crack?

learn: The flag of the United States is red, white and blue.
It has 50 stars, one for each state.
It has 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies.
check: How many stars are on the flag?
How many stripes are on the flag?
lessons.try: Draw the American flag. Count the stripes.

learn: The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
It is strong and free, and it lives only in North America.
Its head has white feathers, not no feathers.
lessons.try: Draw a bald eagle with its white head.

learn: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor.
She holds a torch high to welcome people to America.
She was a gift from France.
check: The Statue of Liberty holds a...
lessons.try: Pose like the Statue of Liberty with a pretend torch.

learn: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia.
It is a symbol of freedom.
It has a big crack.
check: The Liberty Bell is a symbol of...
The Liberty Bell has a big...
lessons.try: Draw the Liberty Bell and its crack.

learn: The White House is where the president lives and works.
It is in Washington, D.C., our nation's capital.
It is painted white.
check: Who lives in the White House?
lessons.try: Draw the White House.

learn: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise to be loyal to our country.
We stand, face the flag and put our right hand over our heart.
Many schools say it every morning.
check: For the pledge, we face the...
Our right hand goes over our...
lessons.try: Practice standing for the pledge with your hand over your heart.

learn: Our national anthem is The Star-Spangled Banner.
It is a song about the flag.
People stand when it is played, often at sports games.
lessons.try: Listen to The Star-Spangled Banner and stand.

learn: Mount Rushmore is a mountain with four presidents' faces carved in it.
The faces are Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln.
It is in South Dakota.
check: How many faces are on Mount Rushmore?
Which president is on Mount Rushmore?
lessons.try: Find South Dakota on a map of the United States.

learn: George Washington was the first president of the United States.
He is called the father of our country.
His face is on the one-dollar bill and the quarter.
check: He is called the father of our...
lessons.try: Find Washington's face on a quarter.

learn: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president.
He helped end slavery, so all people could be free.
His face is on the penny and the five-dollar bill.
lessons.try: Find Lincoln on a penny.

learn: Arizona has its own symbols too.
The state flag has a copper star and red and yellow rays like a sunset.
The state bird is the cactus wren, and the state flower is the saguaro cactus blossom.
check: The star on the Arizona flag is...
lessons.try: Draw the Arizona flag.

learn: Symbols stand for our country: the flag, the bald eagle, the Statue of Liberty and the Liberty Bell.
We honor our country with the pledge and the anthem.
Washington and Lincoln are famous presidents.
check: The flag has how many stars?
lessons.try: Make a book of American symbols with one on each page.

learn: A celebration is a happy time to remember something important.
People celebrate with food, music, games and family.
Birthdays are celebrations of the day someone was born.
check: A happy time to remember something important
lessons.try: Tell how you celebrate a birthday.

learn: On July 4 we celebrate Independence Day, the country's birthday, often with parades and fireworks.
Thanksgiving is a day to be thankful and share a meal.
Some days honour people, like Martin Luther King Jr. Day.
check: What do people do on Thanksgiving?
Share a meal and give thanks
lessons.try: Draw a picture of a celebration you have been to.

learn: Families around the world have many holidays.
People may celebrate a new year, a harvest, a festival of lights or a religious holiday.
Learning about other celebrations helps us understand and respect each other.
check: A new year or a harvest
To understand and respect each other
Do all families celebrate the same holidays?
lessons.try: Ask a friend or neighbour about a holiday their family celebrates.

learn: People everywhere celebrate birthdays, but in different ways.
In Mexico, children may break a piñata. In China, long noodles wish a long life.
In many places, people sing and share cake.
check: In Mexico, children may break a...
Long noodles wish for a long...
Do people everywhere celebrate birthdays the same way?
lessons.try: Ask a friend how their family celebrates birthdays.

learn: Thanksgiving is a holiday in November.
Families share a big meal and give thanks.
It remembers a harvest feast shared by Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people in 1621.
check: The first feast was shared by Pilgrims and the...
lessons.try: Make a list of five things you are thankful for.

learn: Independence Day is July 4.
It is the birthday of the United States, from 1776.
People celebrate with parades, picnics and fireworks.
check: It is the birthday of our...
lessons.try: Draw a Fourth of July parade.

learn: Martin Luther King Jr. Day is in January.
Dr. King worked so that all people would be treated fairly.
He shared a dream that people of every color would be friends.
lessons.try: Draw your dream for a kinder world.

learn: Many families celebrate holidays in winter.
Christmas, Hanukkah and Kwanzaa are winter holidays.
Hanukkah has a menorah with candles. Kwanzaa has a kinara with seven candles.
check: A Kwanzaa kinara has how many candles?
lessons.try: Learn about a winter holiday your family does not celebrate.

learn: Lunar New Year is celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and many other places.
Families clean their homes, share meals and give red envelopes.
Lion and dragon dances bring good luck.
check: Lunar New Year gifts come in...
Families ___ their homes before the new year.
lessons.try: Make a paper dragon or a red envelope.

learn: Diwali is the festival of lights, celebrated in India and around the world.
Families light small lamps called diyas.
People make colorful patterns called rangoli.
check: Small lamps lit on Diwali are called...
lessons.try: Draw a rangoli pattern with bright colors.

learn: Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead, is celebrated in Mexico.
Families remember loved ones who have died with flowers, photos and favorite foods.
Marigolds and sugar skulls are part of the celebration.
check: Día de los Muertos is celebrated in...
lessons.try: Draw a marigold flower.

learn: Eid al-Fitr is a celebration at the end of the month of Ramadan.
Muslim families pray, wear new clothes, share sweets and visit family.
It is a time of giving to people in need.
check: Eid comes at the end of...
Eid is a time of giving to...
lessons.try: Learn one way families celebrate Eid.

learn: Our class may have families with many different celebrations.
Learning about them helps us understand each other.
We can respect celebrations that are different from ours.
check: We can ___ celebrations different from ours.
Do all families celebrate the same holidays?
lessons.try: Share one celebration your family enjoys with the class.

learn: Many celebrations have special foods.
Turkey at Thanksgiving, tamales at Christmas in many Mexican families, mooncakes at the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Food brings people together.
lessons.try: Help cook or bake a celebration food with your family.

learn: People around the world celebrate many holidays.
Celebrations have special foods, lights, music and traditions.
We learn about and respect each other's celebrations.
lessons.try: Make a celebrations calendar showing five holidays.
